To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) morphological knowledge is an important resource for reading and spelling accuracy in children; (2) morphological knowledge facilitates reading and spelling of pseudowords; (3) morphological knowledge helps reading but not spelling of low-frequency words; (4) morphological structure facilitates reading of words with high-frequency roots and low-frequency suffixes; (5) morphological structure does not facilitate reading of words with low-frequency roots and high-frequency suffixes; and (6) spelling of words with
morphological information is useful for both reading and writing, even in a transparent orthography such as Italian.
morphological knowledge facilitates reading and spelling in Italian children, but it does so to a different extent depending on the type of task and the age of the children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of morphology and the development of reading and spelling skills in children learning a regular orthography, such as Italian.
the role of morphology on reading and spelling accuracy in Italian children and with the effect of school experience on morphological facilitation.
the role of morphology on spelling performance and its relation to reading performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the role of morphology is more important for spelling than for reading in Italian, but the role of morphology for spelling is more evident in the case of pseudowords than for low-frequency words, while the opposite is true for reading.
the role of morphology as a facilitative factor in reading and spelling in transparent orthographies is a function of word frequency and of the task under investigation.
the role of morphology is more evident in transparent orthographies than in opaque ones, and that morphological facilitation is a function of task and of the level of development of reading skills.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
morphological knowledge is important for reading and spelling in Italian children.
the effect of morphological knowledge on spelling and reading performance is a function of the orthographic transparency of the language and the type of task.

morphological information is an important source of information for the reading and spelling of both transparent and opaque orthographies, and that the use of this information may be more important for children with less experience in the reading and writing of their native language.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the morphological structure of words is an important source of information in the processing of written language, even in orthographies such as Italian where the print-to-sound and sound-to-print correspondences are highly regular.
, even in transparent orthographies such as Italian, children benefit from the presence of morphology, which can be used to support both reading and spelling.
the morphological structure of a word is useful for reading and spelling in transparent orthographies, but its role may be more prominent in the early stages of literacy acquisition.
